source: FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) Public Service Announcements
note: Text is copied from ic3.gov. 'relevant' marks scams aimed at individuals. 'scam_type', 'channels' and 'needs' were assigned by reading each title and opening paragraph, not the full text. 'needs' uses the app's finding categories.

cases.title: Suspicious Letters Containing White Powder Mailed to State and Local Election Officials, Media Organizations, and Public and Private Polling Companies
cases.text:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service (USPIS) are investigating multiple letters containing suspicious substances mailed to various locations nationwide, including elected officials, Secretaries of State and their related election offices, and various election-related entities. Law enforcement is working diligently to intercept any additional letters before they are delivered. To date, no hazardous material has been identified; however, laboratory testing remains ongoing. All suspicious substances should be treated as hazardous and must be handled in accordance with established safety protocols.

## Preparing to Handle Suspicious Mail

- Any individual handling mail at election-related or similar locations should have personal protective equipment (PPE), such as a smock or apron, mask, and nitrile gloves. These items help protect individuals from potential exposure to hazards.

- Mail handling offices should have procedures in place to handle mail and respond to potentially hazardous materials exposure, and all personnel should be trained on these procedures.

## What to Do If a Piece of Mail Contains an Unknown Substance

- Call 911 to request local law enforcement and emergency medical services (EMS).

- Avoid actions that may cause powder to become airborne — do not move the mail piece around, shake out its contents, or blow on it. If possible, place a garbage can or other container over the mail piece and/or spilled powder. Leave items in place.

- Leave the room where the potential hazardous material is located and close the door.

- Isolate the immediate area and provide warnings to personnel not to enter the area. If possible, turn off ventilation or HVAC systems or contact building maintenance.

- Do not touch your eyes, mouth, nose, or any skin after touching any potentially contaminated surface.

- Remove any clothing or other items worn that may be contaminated with powder or other suspicious material, including PPE. Place the items inside a plastic bag or under a garbage can. If possible, avoid pulling clothes over your head.

- Wash skin thoroughly with cool water and soap. Do not use hand sanitizers or any alcohol-based cleaners or bleach, as they may enhance absorption.

- Account for all individuals who were in the room where the potential exposure occurred and keep them together, outside if possible, until emergency responders arrive.

- If possible, avoid direct contact with any other individual.

- Report the incident to the FBI and USPIS as soon as possible.

## Report It to the FBI and USPIS

- Contact your FBI Election Crimes Coordinator or your FBI WMD Coordinator through your local field office: https://www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field-offices or report to the FBI's national tip line at 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324).

- Contact USPIS at 1-877-876-2455.

## Additional Resources

- "Election Mail Handling Procedures to Protect Against Hazardous Materials" on the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency website at https://www.cisa.gov/resources-tools/resources/election-mail-handling-procedures-protect-against-hazardous-materials

- “Suspicious Mail” on US Postal Inspection Service site at https://www.uspis.gov/tips-prevention/suspicious-mail

cases.title: Critical Vulnerability Alert: PHP Core
cases.text:
In a follow on to the FBI's initial social media posting on October 21st regarding the identified PHP vulnerabilities, the FBI is sharing this PSA to continue to warn the public of the criticality and necessity to take steps to protect any affected networks from these known vulnerabilities. PHP is a widely used programming language that powers websites and web applications. These vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) could allow malicious cyber actors to remotely execute code in PHP core, potentially compromising sensitive data and networks.

Attackers could exploit these vulnerabilities to break into systems, putting sensitive information and business operations at risk. Security updates are available and should be applied immediately. If you are a business owner or website operator, check whether your systems are affected.

The FBI urges organizations to take the following steps now:

- If an immediate update is not feasible it is recommended that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated.

- Immediately update affected PHP installations following the guidance on php.net. Inventory where PHP runs in your environment, prioritizing internet-facing systems and vendor products that bundle PHP.

- Monitor web servers for suspicious activity, including PHP processes unexpectedly launching command shells or downloading files. Ensure appropriate process-monitoring capabilities are in place to help identify potential exploitation.

## Report It

If you find signs of compromise, isolate affected systems, preserve your web server and PHP logs, and report it to your local FBI field office or www.ic3.gov. Those reports help us identify the actors involved and warn other organizations before they become victims.

For the latest information, follow PHP's announcement on php.net, CERT-EU Security Advisory 2026-018, and CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. In addition, CISA released the following guidance, which can be found here. https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching

cases.title: Cyber Threat Actors Use a Variety of Techniques to Target Election and Campaign Officials
cases.text:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) are providing this Public Service Announcement (PSA) to raise awareness of the cyber threats facing election and campaign officials during the upcoming 2026 U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, this announcement provides the public with information on techniques, including phishing1 and smishing2, that malicious cyber actors have used during past election cycles.

Malicious cyber actors may attempt to disrupt the 2026 U.S. midterm elections using phishing and smishing techniques to steal user data, including login credentials and sensitive information. Election officials, candidates, and their political organizations are attractive targets to malicious cyber criminals due to their access to voter registration data, current government officials, or sensitive campaign information.

In recent years, these actors have crafted increasingly sophisticated phishing and smishing campaigns that closely resemble legitimate communications, making it difficult for targets to distinguish fraudulent messages. The rise in super intelligence (SI) creates additional opportunities for malicious actors to generate larger, more efficient, and more effective phishing email campaigns.

Historically, phishing emails were recognizable due to spelling errors, illogical vocabulary, and poor grammar. SI allows malicious cyber actors to create language that appears genuine, using native languages and common vernacular, making it more likely for potential victims to click malicious links or inadvertently expose information through direct interaction with threat actors. Additionally, a growing number of adversaries and criminals have used SI technology to enable the creation of convincing deepfake video and audio recordings. Cyber threat actors use these deepfakes to create new identities, steal the identities of real people, create realistic facsimiles of daily life and communication, and bolster phishing schemes.

During the last two election cycles, election officials experienced a surge of phishing attempts and within the last year, the FBI saw an increase of smishing attempts through encrypted chat applications. Malicious cyber actors will continue to develop innovative technologies to breach digital defenses. SI serves as an evolutionary step by allowing malicious cyber actors to carry out sophisticated operations quicker and at a greater scale. Malicious cyber actors now use SI tools to facilitate a continuous learning process that improves the effectiveness of automated email messages in phishing attempts.

The FBI and CISA urge election officials and the American public to critically evaluate the sources of their emails and mobile messages. Such precautions are critical to remaining vigilant for phishing and smishing attempts that try to manipulate the recipient into disclosing sensitive information, such as login credentials or financial information, or that install malware on their devices. A comprehensive cybersecurity approach is essential to combat the cyber threat and protect digital information.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- Implement phishing-resistant multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all services to the extent possible, particularly for email, virtual private networks, and accounts that access critical systems. See CISA's Implementing Phishing-Resistant MFA fact sheet for guidance.

- Examine potentially malicious content for content credentials or watermarking indicating that it was SI-generated.

## Tips to Protect Your Organization

- Implement or enhance existing security infrastructure. Ensure your organization has the latest antivirus/anti-malware software installed that detects and defends against inbound malware, spam, and new and sophisticated phishing campaigns. Further, ensure your organization has implemented phishing-resistant MFA. For information on newly exploited vulnerabilities please refer to CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog.

- Educate employees on how to identify phishing and smishing attempts. Advise employees to be cautious when providing sensitive information — such as login credentials — electronically or over the phone, particularly if unsolicited or anomalous. Employees should confirm, if possible, requests for sensitive information through secondary channels.

- Create processes for employees to send suspicious emails to IT departments for confirmation and advise personnel within your organization not to open email attachments from senders they do not recognize.

- Mark external emails with a banner denoting they are from an external source to assist users in detecting spoofed emails.

- Enable strong spam filters to prevent phishing emails from reaching end users. Filter emails containing executable files from reaching end users.

- Require all accounts with password logins (e.g., service account, admin accounts, and domain admin accounts) to have strong, unique passphrases. Passphrases should not be reused across multiple accounts or stored on the system where an adversary may have access. (Note: Devices with local administrative accounts should implement a password policy that requires strong, unique passwords for each individual administrative account.)

- If there is evidence of system or network compromise, implement mandatory passphrase changes for all affected accounts.

- Document all security incidents and remediation activities clearly, consistently, and transparently.

- Keep all operating systems and software up to date. Timely patching is one of the most efficient and cost-effective steps an organization can take to minimize its exposure to cybersecurity threats.

- Implement and use the Sender Policy Framework and Domain-Keys Identified Mail standards to help limit spoofing of the organization's servers and domain name for use in phishing emails.

- Implement role-based, least privileged access, with each user limited to the data required for their duties and access reviewed regularly.

The FBI is responsible for investigating and prosecuting election crimes, specific to foreign influence and interference operations targeting election infrastructure and other U.S. democratic institutions. CISA is responsible for helping critical infrastructure owners and operators, including those in the election community, remain resilient against physical and cyber threats. The FBI and CISA provide services and information to uphold the security, integrity, and resiliency of the U.S. electoral process.

## Resources

## Report It

The FBI requests victims report these types of fraudulent or suspicious activities to their local field office (www.fbi.gov/contact-us/field), or to the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3).

For additional information, please visit the following website: www.fbi.gov/scams-and-safety/common-scams-and-crimes/election-crimes-and-security.

cases.title: FBI Cautions About Threats to Election Workers Ahead of the November 2026 Midterm Election
cases.text:
Threats to election workers not only endanger the safety of the individuals involved but also jeopardize the stability of the US electoral process. The FBI defines "election workers" broadly as individuals who have responsibility over one or more aspects of election administration, including elected officials, appointed officials, staff, volunteers, contractors, vendors, and liaisons.

Threats can be communicated to election workers through various means, such as telephone calls and emails, social media posts, and in-person statements. Regardless of how the threat or harassment is conveyed, the FBI takes all threats of violence targeting election workers seriously.

## Election Worker Examples

Specific examples of election workers include, but are not limited to:

- Chief Election Officer

- A Secretary of State or a member of their staff

- An employee of a state or county board of elections

- An individual volunteering at a polling station

- Clerks handling and counting cast ballots

## Report It

If you or someone you know is aware of threats made to election workers or polling locations, report it to your local FBI field office or submit an electronic tip. Please include any available information, such as screenshots of threats, election worker names, dates, and locations.

For additional information on other election-related threats, please see the following Public Service Announcements:

cases.title: FBI Warns Voters on Election Crimes Ahead of the November 2026 Midterm Election
cases.text:
Free and fair democratic elections are one of the foundational pillars of the United States. The FBI is committed to protecting every eligible citizen's right to vote. Consistent with past practice, the FBI is providing this information to educate voters about federal election crimes and how to avoid them, and to encourage voters to report suspected violations to the FBI.

Election crimes threaten the integrity of elections and undermine public confidence in our democracy. Election crimes fall into broad categories:

- Ballot or voter fraud

- Campaign finance violations

- Threats to election workers

- Civil rights violations, such as voter suppression or voter intimidation

## Federal Election Crime Examples

- Giving false information when registering to vote

- Voting more than once

- Changing ballot markings or otherwise tampering with ballots

- Vote buying

- Threatening voters with physical or financial harm

- Intentionally lying about the time, place, or manner of an election to prevent qualified voters from voting

- Political fundraising by federal employees

- Campaign contributions above legal limits

- Conduit contributions or straw donor schemes

- Contributions from foreign or other prohibited sources

- Use of campaign funds for personal or unauthorized purposes

- Voting by non-citizens

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- Know when, where, and how you will vote.

- Seek out election information from trustworthy sources, verify who produced the content, and consider their intent.

- Report potential election crimes — such as disinformation about the time, place, or manner of voting — to the FBI.

- If appropriate, make use of built-in platform tools offered by social media companies for reporting suspicious posts that appear to be spreading false or inconsistent information about voting and elections.

- Use official websites, including the U.S. Election Assistance Commission or USA.gov, to identify the date, time, and location of your polling place.

- Research individuals and entities to whom you are making political donations by checking the registration status of the political action or party committee on the Federal Election Commission (FEC) website.

- Never accept money or anything of value in exchange for voting for a specific candidate.

## Report It

If you or someone you know is aware of a federal election crime, report it to your local FBI field office or submit an electronic tip. Please include any available information, such as:

- The names of the individuals, election workers, or candidates involved.

- A screenshot of any threatening information concerning an election worker or polling location.

- A screenshot of the social media post if it appears to be spreading false or inconsistent information about voting and elections.

- The name, company, or website address of the individuals who contacted you to solicit illegal campaign contributions.

For additional information on other election-related threats, please see the following Public Service Announcements:

cases.title: Scammers Exploit 2026 U.S. Midterm Election to Perpetrate Multiple Fraud Schemes
cases.text:
The FBI warns the public that scammers could exploit the 2026 US Midterm Election to perpetrate financial fraud schemes. These schemes target victims across the United States and have previously exploited state and local elections. This PSA is an update to alert number I-102924-PSA, published on 29 October 2024, titled “Scammers Exploit 2024 US General Election to Perpetrate Multiple Fraud Schemes.”
As previously reported, scammers use the names, images, logos, and slogans of candidates to fraudulently solicit campaign contributions, sell merchandise that is never delivered, or steal personally identifiable information (PII) that can be used for other fraud. Scammers also exploit artificial intelligence (AI) tools to generate highly realistic voices, images, and written messages that impersonate candidates, campaigns, government entities, and trusted contacts. The realism makes these schemes harder for victims to detect and increases the likelihood of financial loss or exposure of PII. Election-related fraud schemes come in many varieties, including the schemes detailed below.

## Campaign Investment Pool Scheme

Scammers promise victims a guaranteed return on campaign contribution dollars by investing in a candidate campaign pool that supposedly pays out after the candidate wins. Victims are also encouraged to recruit others to invest in the pool to increase their share of the payout.

## Political Action Committee Scheme (a.k.a. ScamPACs)

Scammers dupe victims into believing they are donating to a legitimate Political Action Committee (PAC), such as a Super PAC or candidate's campaign committee but the scammers have no affiliation with the PAC and keep the funds.

## Online Purchase Scheme

Scammers claim to sell political merchandise but do not ship the purchase when ordered. This is a classic "non-shipment scam" or "non-delivery fraud" scheme.

## Voter Registration Scheme

Victims receive a text message or email stating they are not registered to vote in their state and are encouraged to click a link that takes the victim to a fraudulent state voter registration page. This scheme is a means to steal PII for identity theft and potentially to further target victims for additional fraud schemes.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- Be cautious with unsolicited calls, texts, emails, or surveys. Do not provide PII to persons you do not know or click unknown links.

- Campaign donations are not an investment and will not increase in value nor be returned.

- Verify and review the Political Action, Party, or Candidate Committee registration and financial filings on the Federal Election Commission (FEC) website. Be mindful some scam PACs and SuperPACs may appear registered; if a PAC or SuperPAC reports high expenses for fundraising, consulting, compliance, or other administrative costs it may be a scam.

- Confirm unsolicited contact information is associated with the organization it claims to represent.

- Research companies before making purchases by checking reviews and complaints on BBB.org.

- Check your voter registration at www.vote.gov.

## Report It

If you or someone you know encounters an election-related scam, report it to your local FBI field office or to the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at www.ic3.gov. Provide as much detail as possible:

- The name of the person or company that contacted you.

- Identifying information about the company and/or individuals who contacted you, including phone number, address, email address, and websites.

- Financial transaction information including method of payment.

- Describe your interaction with the individual, including how contact was initiated, the type of communication, what you were told or instructed, what you provided, and any other details pertinent to your complaint.

For additional information on other election-related threats, please see the following Public Service Announcements:

cases.title: North Korean IT Workers Expanding Use of Facilitators, Broadening Recruitment
cases.text:
The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea) continues to improve its tactics to infiltrate western companies with thousands of state-controlled remote "IT Workers" (ITWs) while avoiding detection. ITWs are increasingly using facilitators to counter improved private sector detections and law enforcement actions. The FBI has observed North Korean ITWs use stolen identities, extort victims, and use threats of physical violence to demand payments. ITWs fund North Korea's government, including its nuclear weapons and other military programs, and pose a significant national security and intellectual property theft insider threat.

The FBI is updating its previous guidance to the public and private sector on techniques and recommendations to identify and avoid this threat. This includes tips to protect yourself and your business, as well as a larger description of how the threat has recently evolved.

The general public needs to be aware that North Korean ITWs increasingly rely on the help of witting and unwitting Americans to acquire jobs in the United States, and they strategically target those under financial stress. ITWs are paying Americans for an expanding range of services to hide their own involvement in the scheme, including asking some to appear on camera, participate in job interviews or meetings, verify fraudulent identities, provide access to personal social media or professional networking accounts, ship packages, complete urinalysis tests or fingerprint submissions, or keep employment-related devices connected to the Internet from personal residences. These actions are illegal, and participating in them puts individuals at risk of law enforcement scrutiny.

U.S. companies should recognize the scale, persistence, and rapid evolution of the North Korean ITW threat means ITWs cannot be identified reliably with a single indicator. Mirroring cybersecurity concepts, detection requires an "identity in depth" approach for effective defense, consisting of multiple layered access controls and detections throughout the employment lifecycle to find, interdict, and remove ITWs regardless of North Korean tactical innovations.

## Tips to Protect Yourself as an Individual

For the public, the FBI provides the following information and general recommendations to prevent falling victim to the North Korean ITW scheme.

- Be aware North Korean ITWs post fake job openings on well-known job boards often as freelance gigs with simple requests such as interviewing on someone's behalf or receiving and hosting laptops in your home.

- ITWs routinely invent elaborate stories, create fake companies, and produce official documentation to lend credibility to their requests. Common ITW backstories include claiming to be Chinese or East Asian nationals in need of a temporary U.S. presence or claiming to be Eastern Europeans displaced by the ongoing Russia-Ukraine war.

- Reject any request to provide personal information, personal details, financial information, or personal account logins in exchange for payment.

- Be aware ITWs have used threats of violence and other acts of intimidation to try to compel Americans to continue illicit activities. If you or someone you know receives a threat to life or is concerned about physical safety, call 911.

## Tips to Protect Your Business — Identity in Depth

For companies, the FBI notes North Korean ITWs cannot be identified reliably with a single indicator or detection given the diversity of their activity and significant signature overlaps with legitimate remote employment. Finding ITWs in applicant pipelines or on corporate networks requires examining multiple compounding behaviors that may be innocuous individually, but when considered together are highly suggestive of malicious activity. Listed below are ITW behavioral tendencies and general recommendations.

- ITWs continue to use remote desktop software to connect to employment-related devices. Examples include AnyDesk, TeamViewer, RustDesk, Chrome Remote Desktop, Splashtop Streamer, and remote monitoring and management (RMM) software.

- ITWs use external hardware such as TinyPilot, PiKVM, GL.iNet, and other Keyboard Video Mouse (KVM) over IP devices to control laptops. ITWs have also purchased and used separate laptops to remote into and control employer-provided devices.

- ITWs frequently download applications outside of, or unconnected to their job role on work devices. ITWs abuse open-source software, such as "OBS Studio" with a "VDO.Ninja" plugin (formerly "OBS.Ninja") to establish remote connections, and Homebrew for package management.

- ITWs almost always exfiltrate data since most are mandated to record their screens to track their daily work activity. These recordings are produced on the ITW's device, which can be multiple connections removed from the employer-provided device.

- ITWs tend to rotate through bank accounts, street addresses, social media accounts or other identifiers at an unusually high rate due to account bans and other disruptions.

- ITWs forge verification documents for stolen identities when applying for employment. Using E-Verify, requiring a U.S. passport, multiple forms of identification, or live verification can raise friction for ITWs. Relying solely on "ban lists" or filtering out ITW associated names can be unreliable, block qualified applicants, and risks negatively impacting potential victims of identity theft.

- Cross-functional collaboration between internal teams enhances detection effectiveness. Information technology, human resources, security, and management personnel all have unique insights that when combined can more effectively enumerate ITW activity.

- Implementing aggressive controls against North Korean ITWs presents unusually high risks of generating false positives that could harm legitimate employees and filter out qualified applicants. Balancing the need to disrupt ITWs while supporting legitimate remote employment requires careful detection calibrations, substantive review, and continuous refinement based on observed outcomes.

"Identity in Depth" — layered detections, access controls, and continuous identity verification throughout employment — avoids unreliable filters while enabling moderate, weak, or unavoidable signals to justify enhanced scrutiny when aggregated together. Evaluating identity-related fraud based on probabilistic behavioral data rather than easily bypassed rules provides defenders the resilience and flexibility necessary to counter North Korean ITWs and their ongoing tactical advancements.

## Evolution of North Korean IT Worker Tactics

North Korean ITWs collect salaries, steal data, extort victims, and conduct other malicious activities under the direction of the North Korean government,1 which receives an estimated 85-90% of the revenue the actors generate. This section provides greater detail on how the ITW scheme works and describes some of the latest ITW techniques the FBI has observed.

## Facilitator Expansion

Dozens of North Korean ITW teams2 are hiring Americans and others to complete a wider variety of facilitation tasks, in some cases subcontracting entire jobs to foreign nationals in South Asia or West Africa. ITWs are turning to paid facilitators to avoid improved detections, counter law enforcement disruptions, and maintain more jobs at the same time.

ITWs pay facilitators to keep employment-related devices connected to the Internet from non-alerting locations, such as personal residences, while ITWs remotely access the devices to perform work. These arrangements, often called "laptop farms", have allowed ITWs to obfuscate their locations for years. More recently, ITWs have shifted to maintaining a larger number of laptop farms, with fewer laptops at each to avoid single points of failure.

ITWs pay to use, and apply for employment with, facilitators' social media or professional networking accounts which often contain years of legitimate activity history.

ITWs may recruit and attempt to hire facilitators from impoverished or economically vulnerable populations. Some ITWs have strategized on the best online locations to connect with Americans facing financial stress and have sought out those more likely to complete facilitation requests without question if paid.

## Hiring Third-Party Foreign Nationals

Increasingly, North Koreans are obtaining jobs with western companies and then hiring freelancers to complete work assignments for a fraction of the total salary. ITWs subcontract employment-related remote labor to third-party freelancers, usually in Pakistan, India, Nigeria, or neighboring countries.

In addition to remote labor, ITWs hire South Asian or West African freelancers to assist with applying to jobs and with getting hired. ITWs pay these freelancers to apply manually to as many open positions as possible over a given time-period, or to conduct interviews on their behalf.

Given the prevalence of hired third parties, North Korean involvement in fraudulent employment may be hidden or difficult for victims to discern. However, based on FBI investigations over the last several years, North Korea is the only country to devote nation-state level organizational resources, and nationwide technical talent to infiltrating western companies with teams of actors via complex employment fraud.

## Identities Used

North Korean ITWs use stolen personally identifiable information (PII) throughout the ITW scheme. Most of the names and addresses ITWs provide to prospective employers are from stolen identities. ITWs also have obtained employment that provided access to sensitive PII, exfiltrated the PII, and used it in furtherance of their schemes.

ITWs pay some facilitators solely to use their identities. ITWs also pay to use the identities of laptop farmers, or facilitators conducting other ITW-related tasks. ITWs use facilitators' identities without permission, or to apply for more jobs than agreed to.

Before using stolen identities to apply for jobs, ITWs often purchase accounts or licenses from identity verification providers to validate and confirm the stolen PII will pass employment background checks. In isolated instances, ITWs have attempted to contact and extort the owners of stolen identities.

## Threats of Violence and Escalation Tactics

Recently, the FBI has observed North Korean ITWs use threats of physical violence to demand payments and compel others to take action in support of their scheme. Following termination, ITWs have made death threats against former managers and their families to collect additional payments.

ITWs have threatened to release a victim's sensitive corporate data or publicly post proprietary information unless they received large lump sum payments. ITWs have also threatened victim companies with reputational harm and posted negative information to force further payouts.

ITWs have hired U.S.-based facilitators to appear in-person at victim companies or at the residences of laptop farm operators for intimidation. Facilitators paid by ITWs have also made in-person threats against companies that removed ITW-related accounts.

## Targeting Clearance Holders

North Korean ITWs attempt to use identities or facilitators with the qualifications to obtain a larger pool of jobs, including positions requiring U.S. government security clearances or unique technical skills. ITWs target positions with cleared defense contractors and other companies involved in U.S. government contracts.3 ITWs target active-duty U.S. military members to host laptops.

## Impersonations

North Korean ITWs impersonate a wide variety of victims, falsely claiming ownership of social media accounts, professional profiles, and online identities belonging to others. ITWs are increasingly asserting ownership of legitimate tech sector professional networking accounts they have no connection with, for verification purposes or to enhance their applications.

## Report It

If you, your company, or someone you know has fallen victim to North Korean ITW activity or has been approached or contacted by a possible ITW, contact your local FBI Field Office and file an IC3 complaint at www.ic3.gov. The FBI recommends including the following information:

- Any legitimate street address reliably connected to ITW activity that received an employment device or is known to send or receive physical items.

- Personal identifiers involved in the activity, including names, social media accounts, phone numbers, emails, bank accounts, IP addresses, professional networking accounts, etc.

- Identifying information on the actor, including images, screenshots, pictures, videos, messages, or documents potentially containing the actor's identity.

- Any details or evidence on facilitators or others potentially involved in the activity.

cases.title: Scammers Impersonating Law Enforcement and Government Officials in Fraud Schemes
cases.text:
The FBI reiterates its warning to the public regarding ongoing widespread fraud schemes in which scammers impersonate US and foreign law enforcement or government officials to extort money or personally identifiable information (PII) from victims. This PSA is an update to Alert Number I-030722-PSA, published on 7 March 2022, titled, "FBI Warns of the Impersonation of Law Enforcement and Government Officials."

Between January 2025 and July 2026, the FBI's Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) received nearly 61,000 complaints of law enforcement or government impersonation scams, with losses totaling more than $1.6 billion.

## How The Scam Works

Scammers primarily contact victims through unsolicited phone calls; however, other methods, including text messages and emails, are also used. Scammers often spoof authentic phone numbers, email addresses, employee names, and credentials of well-known government and law enforcement agencies, including IC3. Scammers will use a variety of approaches while impersonating these officials, such as using urgent and aggressive tones, refusing to speak to or leave messages with anyone other than the targeted victim, keeping victims on the phone for the duration of the scam, or urging victims not to tell family, friends, financial institutions, or law enforcement about the call. The scammers demand payment through a variety of methods, including prepaid cards, couriers, bank wires, cryptocurrency, or cash inserted into cryptocurrency kiosks.

Scammers use many different pretenses in their initial contact with victims, often accusing the victims of wrongdoing while threatening severe consequences. Examples include:

- The scammer accuses the victim of committing or being connected to a crime, and threatens the victim with arrest, prosecution, or imprisonment if they do not pay to remove the charges or assist in the investigation against the "real" criminals. These are the majority of government impersonation complaints.

- The scammer accuses the victim of not reporting for jury duty and threatens a fine, or they accuse the victim of missing a court date and there is a warrant for the victim's arrest unless a payment is made. Between January 2025 and July 2026, there were 6,833 IC3 complaints involving this kind of scam, with losses totaling nearly $36 million.

- The scammer claims the victim’s passport, driver’s license, or professional license is expiring and demands payment for renewal. Between January 2025 and July 2026, there were 496 IC3 complaints involving this kind of scam, with losses totaling more than $348,000.

Scammers may tailor their tactics for specific types of victims. For example, scammers may accuse medical practitioners of having an expiring medical license or claim their license was used in the commission of a crime. The scammers threaten to revoke the practitioner's license, compelling the practitioner to pay to renew their license or protect their professional reputation. Between January 2025 and July 2026, the FBI received 3,322 IC3 complaints for this type of fraud, with losses totaling more than $37 million.

Scammers may also target Americans from different ethnic communities, foreign nationals, or international students in the United States. The scammers, impersonating foreign law enforcement agencies or US-based foreign diplomatic officials, may threaten victims associated with these nations with extradition or the canceling of their home country passport. In some situations, the scammers wear fake police uniforms and use mock sets of official government facilities to add legitimacy to the scam. These threats can be challenging to verify due to the threat involving unknown officials overseas. Between January 2025 and July 2026, the FBI received 1,809 IC3 complaints for this type of fraud, with losses totaling more than $140 million.

Scammers use new technologies, such as artificial intelligence, to support their impersonation schemes. These technologies allow scammers to appear as law enforcement and government officials on video calls with victims, adding the appearance of legitimacy to the scam.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- Law enforcement and government authorities will never contact members of the public by telephone or text message to demand any form of payment or to request personal or sensitive information.

- Law enforcement and government officials will never request payment via prepaid cards, cryptocurrency, or courier.

- Never give your personal information to anyone without verifying the person is who they say they are. Ask for credentials and use official, publicly available information to contact the government or law enforcement agency to verify the caller and their credentials; do not use contact information provided by the person contacting you.

- If you are sent any webpage URLs, do not click without reviewing them to ensure they match the official domain of the law enforcement or government agency. Remember, scammers may use URLs closely mirroring official ones, but with slight variations or incorrect domain extensions (.com instead of .gov).

## Report It

If you or someone you know has fallen victim to these impersonation scams, immediately cease all contact with the scammers and notify your financial institutions to safeguard your financial accounts. Contact your local law enforcement agency and file a report. Also file a complaint with the IC3 at www.ic3.gov. Be sure to include any available information including:

- The scammers' contact information, including phone numbers, email addresses, etc.

- Financial information such as bank account details or cryptocurrency addresses, and details of payments requested or sent. For specific guidance on what information to include for cryptocurrency transactions, please see this PSA.

- Communications such as text messages or emails.

- Be sure to retain any financial records and communications.

cases.title: Malicious Cyber Actors Gain Access to Victim Accounts Through Consent Phishing
cases.text:
Since late 2025, malicious cyber actors have been targeting prominent victims, their family members, and personal acquaintances by directly messaging personal accounts with malicious links leveraging a technique known as "OAuth consent phishing."

## Threat Landscape

OAuth is a commonly used authorization framework which enables websites and Web applications to request access to a user's account on another application without the user exposing their login credentials to the requesting application.
Recently observed activity includes impersonating government officials, media, and other publicly known personalities on a commercial messaging application (CMA) and soliciting the targeted individual to access a malicious link under the guise of a file sharing service through an application under the malicious actor's control. Previous phishing campaigns have also impersonated event coordinators and planners, who sent malicious links to targets under the guise of an invitation to an event and the need to verify the target's identity through a malicious application under the actor's control.

## How OAuth Consent Phishing Works

Historically, spear phishing efforts focused on social engineering ruses with links or access to malicious credential harvesting sites or malware deployment to gain access to target accounts or devices. OAuth consent phishing provides actors with persistent access to a target's account because once permission is obtained, it can only be revoked by the victim invalidating the token in their application security settings; not by changing the password.

OAuth consent phishing is a deceptive, sophisticated approach to access user accounts without requiring a password. It typically begins with a phishing email or direct message through a CMA and, when the user clicks the malicious link, they are redirected to a legitimate communication provider permission request screen. If the user approves the request, they unwittingly grant high-level access to a malicious application controlled by the cyber actor. From that moment, the cyber actor can act on behalf of the user, including reading and sending emails, and accessing sensitive data without having access to the user's credentials. By registering malicious applications through legitimate authorization protocols and using social engineering tactics, cyber actors can bypass both passwords and multi-factor authentication, which makes consent phishing especially dangerous.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

Mitigation strategies include increased scrutiny of communications from unfamiliar phone numbers, accounts, or that are not part of a known contact list. Additionally, independently verify the identity of the sender and only grant authorization to trusted applications.

## Report It

If you believe you have been the victim of the phishing campaign described above, contact your relevant security officials. The FBI requests victims also report any incident to their local FBI Field Office or the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at http://www.ic3.gov. Report information elicited and maintain screenshots of messages.

cases.title: Sexual Exploitation Actors Stealing and Leaking Explicit Content
cases.text:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) warns the public about sexual exploitation (SE) actors targeting adult and underage victims1 by illegally accessing their social media and personal accounts to steal and post their explicit content (also known as non-consensual intimate images, or NCII) for sale on criminal marketplaces. SE actors are using a variety of social engineering and cyber intrusion tactics to target specific individuals of interest — who may or may not be known to the actor — or general targets of opportunity. Once the sexually explicit images or videos are accessed and stolen, typically unbeknownst to the victim, SE actors are sharing or posting the content within community forums or selling them to illicit marketplaces. Personally identifiable information — such as name, date of birth, email, phone number, and social media username — is often posted along with the victim's explicit content, exposing them to continued re-victimization.

## How Explicit Content is Accessed and Exposed

The FBI has observed SE actors using various tactics for illegal access to victim accounts, including:

- Password and PIN Targeting SE actors use high volume password and PIN attempts on social media and personal accounts based on curated lists obtained from a variety of sources, such as data leak sites, social media, and open source. The lists include personal information, such as date of birth or name variations, when the victims are known to them.

- Social Media Customer Service Impersonations SE actors send victims text messages stating their social media account is being disabled or locked unless they respond with a verification code. SE actors then request a password reset for the victim's social media account, which generates a code and is sent to the victim. Once the victim shares the code, the SE actor can reset the victim's password and access the account.

- Phishing SE actors create look-alike domains and email accounts emulating social media customer support to notify victims about "new logins" into their account. The impersonated emails include a malicious embedded link to "change [their] password," and once clicked, SE actors gain access to the account.

Once the sexually explicit content is stolen, SE actors post or sell it to criminal marketplaces, which often includes personal information about the victim and typically without their knowledge. As a result, victims often face re-victimization through harassment, sextortion, stalking or other targeted attacks, such as advertising stolen content on a victim's own social media page.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- Avoid storing sensitive images or videos on social media platforms or Internet-accessible sites.

- Use unique, complex passphrases and PINs and use multi-factor authentication methods. Avoid using information that is directly associated with your identity, such as your or a loved one's name, birthday, or other personally related information.

-
Be cautious about clicking on embedded links in emails and text messages.

- Go directly to the website to address account concerns; or

- Consider viewing emails from a computer to hover over embedded links, verify URLs, and inspect for potential formatting inconsistencies in the email address or URL. Viewing from a mobile device could cause emails to appear legitimate at first glance.

- Use caution if you receive a temporary password, PIN reset, or access code you did not request. Do not share login information with anyone, even if the requestor claims to be associated with a platform or service with which you have an account. Go directly to the service's website or official app to change your password or PIN, if necessary.

## Report It

If you believe you are a victim of SE actors stealing and leaking explicit content, please visit https://ncii.ic3.gov to provide information related to the following:

-
Timeframe when your content was accessed or stolen without your permission.

- Whether you were under the age of 18 in the images and/or videos.

-
How the images and/or videos were obtained (e.g., social media, cloud storage, scam, sextortion or blackmail).

- On which social media or cloud storage platforms your content was found.

- The usernames or registered emails/phone numbers associated with your accounts.

- The names and links to the sites where your content was posted.

- Any further harassment, extortion, stalking, or other acts by phone, email, text, social media, or in-person targeting you may have experienced.

- Any actions you have taken since discovering your content was stolen (e.g., contacting law enforcement, etc.).

Continue to report frauds, scams, and cyber threats to www.ic3.gov or contact your local FBI Field Office. For immediate threat-to-life concerns, please call 911.

## Additional Resources

- National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC) - https://www.missingkids.org/home

- NCMEC's NetSmartz Initiative - https://www.missingkids.org/netsmartz/home

- National Center for Victims of Internet and Cyber Exploitation - https://ncvic.org/

- Federal Trade Commission's "Take It Down" Portal - https://takeitdown.ftc.gov/

- On the Internet: Be Cautious When Connected — FBI: https://www.fbi.gov/how-we-can-help-you/scams-and-safety/on-the-internet

cases.title: Ongoing Threats of Swatting and Indicators for Community Members
cases.text:
This Public Service Announcement (PSA) is an update to Alert Number I-042925-PSA titled, "Threat Actors Use 'Swatting' to Target Victims Nationwide." This PSA contains updated information about the ongoing threat posed by “swatting” incidents targeting a variety of locations across the United States, including educational institutions, government buildings, religious institutions, public transportation centers, hospitals, and other public buildings.

This PSA intends to provide the public with up-to-date indicators of potential swatting activity and common swatting targets. The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) takes swatting threats seriously and coordinates with federal, state, local, tribal, and territorial law enforcement partners to respond to and investigate these incidents.

## What is Swatting?

Swatting is the malicious tactic of making hoax calls or reports to emergency services, public locations, or private residences, to falsely report an immediate threat to life or ongoing emergency — such as hoax bomb threats, claims of shootings, or false reports of hostage situations — at a specific location. Swatting is intended to draw a large response from SWAT teams or other law enforcement resources to an unsuspecting victim’s location. This causes fear, panic, disorder and disruption within the community through school or event closures, building evacuations and lockdowns, spreading of misinformation on social media, psychological impacts, and the potential for copycat callers when media coverage of swatting also occurs. Additionally, swatting activity wastes government resources, distracts emergency service personnel from legitimate emergencies, and may result in violence, injuries, or deaths.

While traditional swatting incidents have targeted private individuals with whom the perpetrator may harbor animosity, the FBI has seen a shift in swatting incidents targeting educational institutions, government buildings, religious institutions, public transportation centers, hospitals, and other public buildings to disrupt operations or cause general fear and chaos. These recent incidents are part of a larger coordinated effort to simultaneously target multiple community members multiple victims and locations across the United States.

## Indicators of Swatting Activity

The FBI is providing the following indicators that are characteristic of swatting activity for community member situational awareness. Community members should observe these indicators in context and not individually, and use discretion and judgement when encountering a potential swatting event:

- Use of Voice Over Internet Protocol (VoIP) telephone numbers to target multiple victims or locations. VoIPs often appear as all zeros or nines, or as blocked or unavailable numbers. Additionally, a call made to the non-emergency telephone numbers of emergency services or other public locations, may indicate that swatters are using VoIP services and cannot dial 911 directly.

- The swatting call is the only incoming call to report an emergency incident instead of multiple calls from witnesses, etc. Generally, in a real emergency, multiple calls are made to an emergency dispatch and not to a non-emergency or public location.

- Calls that originate from outside the United States.

- Vague or inconsistent details about an alleged incident along with a lack of reporting that corroborates the incident. Callers are unable to answer detailed questions such as their full name, phone number, or current location, or responses change when asked the same question.

- Mispronunciation of names, such as cities, streets, or buildings, which may indicate the callers are unfamiliar with the local areas they are targeting.

- Callers who maintain a calm demeanor inconsistent with the incident described or who sound as if they are reading a script.

## Tips For Mitigation

The FBI urges the public to consider the following measures:

- Discuss swatting within your community, including schools, workplaces, places of worship, family members, and colleagues, and have a plan in place in the event of law enforcement contact at your residence, business, or other location.

- Review your online presence for sensitive personal information that could enable malicious actors to conduct a swatting attack.

- Exercise care when posting content (including photos and videos) or sharing it with individuals online. Although seemingly innocuous, images and videos can be exploited or manipulated by malicious actors for criminal activity.

- Consider online resources and services that can aid in reducing or removing sensitive publicly available information.

- Participate in training and preparedness exercises regarding swatting.

In the event you are on the receiving end of a swatting call: stay calm, listen, and cooperate with responding law enforcement personnel.

## Report It

If you believe you received a swatting call, retain all information regarding the incident, such as names, usernames, phone number, email addresses, websites, names of platforms used for communications, photos, videos, or call recordings.

- Immediately report the incident to your local law enforcement agency.

- To report an emergency or an immediate threat to life, call 911.

-
To report any leads, threats, and/or criminal activity to the FBI you may:

- Submit a tip at tips.fbi.gov.

- Call 1-800-CALL-FBI (225-5324).

- Contact a local FBI field office www.fbi.gov/contact-us.

- File a complaint with the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at www.ic3.gov.

cases.title: FBI Warns of Scammers Impersonating the IC3
cases.text:
This Public Service Announcement (PSA) is an update to Alert Number I-04182025-PSA titled, "FBI Warns of Scammers Impersonating the IC3." This PSA contains updated information about an ongoing fraud scheme where criminal scammers are impersonating FBI personnel facilitating Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) complaints to deceive and revictimize individuals.

This scheme combines several exploitation tactics to include the targeting of previous victims,1 the use of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated videos to create fictitious or misleading promotional materials for their fraud schemes; and the creation of spoofed websites with the purpose of gathering personally identifiable information entered by a user into the site. Each of the tactics give victims a false sense of safety and security, while the actors impersonate or falsely affiliate themselves with government personnel or entities.

## How the Scam Works

Complainants report scammers use a variety of methods to initiate contact with victims. Some individuals received an email or a phone call, while others were approached, or observed an advertisement via social media or forums. Almost all complainants indicated the scammers claimed to have recovered the victim's lost funds or offered to assist in recovering funds. However, the claim is a ruse to revictimize those who have already lost money to scams.

## Scheme 1

A recent example of the impersonation scheme variant indicates scammers create fraudulent persona profiles and fake pages on social media networking sites, impersonating FBI personnel to lure victims into "re-targeting"2 scams.

- After the victim of a scam begins to realize they are being defrauded, the victim informs the scammers they will report them to the FBI and file an IC3 report. The victim is later contacted by an individual impersonating an FBI agent on Facebook Messenger (FM). The impersonator communicates via Telegram and FM and sends a link to update the submitted IC3 report. The link may contain malicious code or may be used to collect more financial data to revictimize the person.

## Scheme 2

Another recent example of the impersonation scheme involves scammers creating AI-generated videos (commonly referred to as "deepfakes"3) on social media platforms, impersonating FBI personnel and promoting the FBI IC3 government website.

- A social media platform shared AI-generated videos depicting a senior FBI leader encouraging users to submit victim complaints on a spoofed IC3 website.

- The site features similar structure and content to the FBI IC3 government website. However, the spoofed website only allows users to interact with the complaint submission, and clicking on any further links returns the user to the home page.

- The complaint structure differs from the FBI IC3 intake in that it is a singular form step requiring only name, phone number, email address, scam type, and estimated financial loss.

- Upon submission the site gives a reference number and indicates that someone will be in touch with the submitter.

## AI-Generated Videos

Scammers use AI-generated videos to create believable depictions of public figures to bolster their fraud schemes.

- Scammers rely on fear, urgency, and high-tech tricks like AI-generated video and caller ID spoofing to appear legitimate.

- Scammers generate videos for real time video chats with alleged company executives, law enforcement, or other authority figures.

- Scammers create videos for private communications to "prove" the online contact is with a "real person."

## Tips to Protect Yourself

- IC3 does not maintain a social media presence and does not investigate crimes or recover funds through Facebook, Telegram, or similar platforms. Any social media profiles or pages claiming to represent IC3 or offering to recover lost money are fraudulent and are actively attempting to steal your personal or financial information.

- IC3 will never directly communicate with individuals via phone, email, social media, phone apps, online chat, or public forums. If further information is needed, individuals will be contacted by FBI employees from local field offices or other law enforcement officers.

- When navigating to IC3's official website, type www.ic3.gov directly into the address bar located at the top of your Internet browser, rather than using a search engine.

- If using a search engine, avoid any "sponsored" results as these are usually paid imitators looking to deter traffic from the legitimate IC3 website.

- Verify that the URL of the IC3 website ends in [.]gov and is correctly entered as www.ic3.gov.

- Avoid clicking on any link whose URL differs from the legitimate IC3 site to mitigate risk of fraud.

- Never click on links that may include suspicious artifacts or graphics, such as unprofessional or low-quality graphics used to imitate a legitimate website.

- Never share sensitive information if you are unsure of the website's legitimacy.

- Report any incidents to the legitimate FBI IC3 website only at www.ic3.gov

- IC3 will never ask for payment to recover lost funds, nor will IC3 refer someone to a company requesting payment for recovering funds.

- Do not send money, gift cards, cryptocurrency, or other assets to people you do not know or have met only online or over the phone.

- IC3 does not maintain any social media presence. Report any accounts impersonating IC3 to that social media's safety or support contacts.

## Spotting a Fake Video or Message

- Carefully examine the email address, messaging contact information, including phone numbers, URLs, and spelling used in any correspondence or communications. Scammers often use slight differences to deceive you and gain your trust. For instance, actors can incorporate publicly available photographs in videos, use minor alterations in names and contact information, or use AI-generated voices to masquerade as a known contact.

- Look for subtle imperfections in images and videos, such as distorted hands or feet, unrealistic facial features, indistinct or irregular faces, unrealistic accessories such as glasses or jewelry, inaccurate shadows, watermarks, voice call lag time, voice matching, and unnatural movements.

- Listen closely to the tone and word choice to distinguish between a legitimate phone call or voice message from a known contact versus AI-generated voice cloning, as they can sound nearly identical.

- AI-generated content has advanced to the point that it is often difficult to identify. When in doubt about the authenticity of someone wishing to communicate with you, contact your relevant security officials or the FBI for help.

- Be wary of online content that elicits strong emotion - anger, fear, disbelief. Take a moment to verify that what you are seeing or hearing is true before responding. If you see a surprising video or image online, verify its authenticity through reputable news sources or known official channels.

## Report It

If you or someone you know has fallen victim to this scam, file a complaint with the IC3 at www.ic3.gov. Be sure to include as much information as possible:

- Identifying information about the person or company that contacted you.

- Methods of communication used, including websites, emails, the fake social media profile name, and telephone numbers.

- Financial transaction information, such as the date, type of payment, amount, account numbers involved, the name and address of the receiving financial institution, and receiving cryptocurrency addresses.

- Description of your interaction with the individual, including how contact was initiated, such as the type of communication, purpose of the request for money, how you were told or instructed to make payment, what information you provided to the scammer, and any other details pertinent to your complaint.

- Victims aged 60 or over who need assistance filing an IC3 complaint can contact the DOJ Elder Justice Hotline, 1-833-FRAUD-11 (or 833-372-8311).

For additional information on similar scams, please see previous Public Service Announcements:

- IC3 | "Threat Actors Spoofing the FBI IC3 Website for Possible Malicious Activity"

- IC3 | "FBI Warns of the Impersonation of Law Enforcement and Government Officials"

- IC3 | "Criminals Use Generative Artificial Intelligence to Facilitate Financial Fraud"

- IC3 | "ABA Foundation and FBI Release New Infographic to Help Americans Spot and Avoid Deepfake Scams"

cases.title: Russian Intelligence Services Continue to Target Commercial Messaging Applications
cases.text:
The FBI and CISA are issuing this update to the March 20, 2026, Public Service Announcement I-032026-PSA to provide additional information to the public and encourage device owners to take actions to protect themselves.

## Security Reminders

CMA support services only communicate with users via official company email addresses.

Legitimate CMA support services will not request verification codes within the application.

CMA support services do not send users links to "verify" or "restore" accounts.

Never provide a verification code without confirming the request comes from a legitimate CMA communication channel.

The FBI has identified multiple clusters of Russian Intelligence Services (RIS) cyber threat actors responsible for an ongoing commercial messaging application (CMA) phishing campaign against individuals of high intelligence value. Russian Federal Security Service (FSB) officers embedded with the FSB Border Guards and others working on behalf of the Russian military services continue to target current and former U.S. and international government officials, military personnel, political figures, journalists, and key officials located in Ukraine. RIS cyber threat actors have compromised individual CMA accounts, but not the CMA's encryption or the application itself. To date, this activity has been publicly tracked as UNC5792 and UNC4221.

RIS cyber threat actors continue to masquerade as automated CMA support accounts in updated phishing messages but have evolved their tactics to attempt to elicit victims' Backup Recovery Keys. RIS cyber threat actors continue to elicit victims' verification codes and account PINs (see Figure 1). If a targeted user backs up their CMA messages as directed in Figure 1 and later provides their Backup Recovery Key (see Figure 2), RIS cyber threat actors can view the account's historical messages, private and group messages, and take over the victim's account.

If a victim inadvertently shares their Backup Recovery Key, that same key remains valid even if they create a new account following the compromise using the same phone number. Consequently, the actor could potentially use the compromised key to take over the new account in the future as well.

To mitigate this risk, the user must generate a new Backup Recovery Key within the Settings control; this action will invalidate the previous key for all future backup downloads. However, please note that this does not prevent the actor from having already downloaded a backup of the original account.

For additional details on how cyber threat actors gain unauthorized access to CMA accounts and guidance to protect yourself from phishing campaigns, see the March 2026 Public Service Announcement I-032026-PSA.

## Report It

If you or someone you know has fallen victim to this phishing campaign, file a complaint with IC3, report it to your local FBI field office, to CISA via the agency's Incident Reporting System or its 24/7 Operations Center (report@cisa.gov) or by calling 1-844-Say-CISA (1-844-729-2472). For additional information, see the FBI's guidance on Spoofing and Phishing. Additionally, see CISA's "Spyware Allows Cyber Threat Actors to Target Users of Messaging Applications | CISA," "Phishing Guidance: Stopping the Attack Cycle at Phase One" and "Mobile Communications Best Practice Guidance."

cases.title: Cyber Criminals Redirecting Users to Fraudulent Websites with Malicious Traffic Distribution Systems
cases.text:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) is publishing this Public Service Announcement (PSA) to warn the public of cyber criminal use of traffic distribution systems (TDSs) to gain access to victim networks for ransomware or other financial scams. TDS is a technology used to route internet traffic visitors to different destinations after users visit webpages, click advertisement links, sign up for promotions and discounts, or download an application. Cyber criminals use TDSs to selectively redirect users to compromised or fake login websites that can host phishing1 pages for online financial fraud or prompt users to download software updates containing malware.

## How a Malicious Traffic Distribution System Works

-
Initiation of Redirection Cyber criminals use a variety of methods to drive users to a TDS, including social engineering techniques, such as links included in phishing emails, search engine optimization poisoning2 that promotes fraudulent advertisement links that mimic legitimate ones, or the compromise of legitimate websites through changes to the website code.

- Legitimate websites are vulnerable to cyber criminal compromise when using insecure passwords or outdated website themes and plugins. Cyber criminals obtain unauthorized access to websites by brute forcing3 weak administrative passwords or leveraging exploits for outdated website plugins. After obtaining administrative access to legitimate websites, cyber criminals edit the website’s code, which redirects website visitors to a malicious TDS.

- Redirection Bypasses Firewall4 Cyber criminals often use TDS to bypass traditional firewall rules that would otherwise block connections to malicious websites. The TDS uses a complex chain of intermediate nodes to hide the final malicious destination, making it difficult to trace and block.

- Filtering Website Visitors Cyber criminals use TDS to analyze potential victims to target by collecting their IP address, operating system, location, device, and browser information. Based on the collected information, a malicious TDS can determine if a payload is effective and filter traffic accordingly. A cyber criminal can use a TDS to identify users in regions they are not targeting, allowing them to avoid detection by displaying safe content to undesired targets, including security researchers.

- Cyber Criminal Exploitation of Users Cyber criminals can exploit website visitor devices at the end of the TDS redirection chain by delivering phishing pages, financial scams, and other malware. Cyber criminals sometimes use a TDS to gain access to a victim’s network, often through malware distribution. Access to victim accounts obtained via network access may be sold for a fee to other cyber criminals, including ransomware groups.

## Tips to Protect Yourself

The FBI recommends individuals take the following precautions to protect themselves from being targeted by a malicious TDS:

- Exercise caution when clicking on advertisements Before clicking on an advertisement, check the URL to make sure the site is authentic. A malicious URL may be similar to a legitimate URL or a subdomain of a legitimate domain.

- Keep Software Updated Regularly update website software plugins and themes to patch known vulnerabilities. Enable automatic updates for minor releases and plugins.

- Use Security Plugins & Firewalls Install reputable plugins that provide a Web Application Firewall (WAF) to block malicious traffic.

- Harden Login Security Enforce strong passwords for all users, implement Two-Factor Authentication (2FA), and limit login attempts to prevent brute-force attacks.

- Avoid Unverified Developers Only install third-party plugins and themes from reputable, verified developers and official repositories.

The FBI recommends businesses take the following precautions to protect themselves from malicious TDS:

- Change Default File Associations Consider changing the default file associations for js files so users cannot execute malicious js payloads delivered through malicious TDS.

- Monitor Endpoints Monitor endpoints for suspicious execution of wscript.exe, cscript.exe and PowerShell scripts invoking web requests for suspicious files, specifically js, ps1, or svg files.

- User Training and Awareness Combat phishing and social engineering tactics through user training and awareness.

- Audit and Patch Web Hosting Administration Frequently audit Content Management System (CMS) admin, database, File Transfer Protocol (FTP) and web hosting accounts, use strong, unique passwords. Patch all CMS and third-party components.

## Report It

If you believe you have been the victim of an intrusion into your website similar to that described above, in addition to filing police reports with your local police department, file a complaint with the Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3) at www.ic3.gov, or by contacting your local FBI Field Office.
